Your shop door in Baarle-Hertog and Baarle-Nassau can sit in two countries at once. White crosses on the pavement show the Belgium-Netherlands border running through streets and houses, with Belgian and Dutch enclaves inside each other.
Your six-month calendar decides who owns Pheasant Island on the Bidasoa river. Spain and France take turns, six months each, and a tiny uninhabited island is the payoff on the map.

Your library card works in two countries at the Haskell Free Library in Vermont and Quebec. A black line on the reading-room floor marks the US-Canada border, and you can see people sit on both sides of it.
Your train track in Belgium's Vennbahn runs through Germany. The old railway line belongs to Belgium, so a Belgian cycle path cuts through German land and leaves German villages on both sides.
Your drive on the Saatse Boot road in Estonia passes through Russia for about 100 metres. Drivers cannot stop or get out, and the map shows a road dipping into Russian land and back.
Your map of Hans Island shows a rock between Canada and Greenland that was split down the middle. After a long 'whisky war' of leaving bottles, Canada and Denmark divided it in 2022.

Your goat-island crisis is real: Spain and Morocco nearly went to war in 2002 over Perejil Island, a rock close to the Moroccan coast. Spanish troops removed a handful of Moroccan soldiers, and the island is a bare rock on the map.

Your Matterhorn border walk can change with the weather. Melting glaciers shifted the Swiss-Italian border near the Matterhorn, and the two countries have agreed to redraw it. The map shows the line moving.
Your map of Sokh in the Fergana Valley shows an Uzbek enclave inside Kyrgyzstan, with Kyrgyz land on every side. It is one of several such pockets in the valley.

Your street in Santana do Livramento, Brazil, runs straight into Rivera, Uruguay. The two towns are one built-up area, and in many places only a row of border markers or a park separates the countries.

Your lane in Sha Tau Kok, Hong Kong, has a street called Chung Ying Street that is split by the border. One side belongs to Hong Kong and the other to mainland China, and border markers stand on the road.

Your British holiday could be on Cyprus. The island has British Sovereign Base Areas at Akrotiri and Dhekelia, and the map shows the UK holding land on a Mediterranean island that is itself an EU country.

Your speed sign flips from miles to kilometres when you cross the Irish border. The road continues unchanged, but Northern Ireland uses mph and the Republic of Ireland uses km/h, which makes the invisible border visible.

Your hug through a fence at Friendship Park, where the US-Mexico border meets the Pacific near San Diego and Tijuana, is real. Families have been able to meet through the mesh, and the fence runs into the sea.
Your Nathu La visit in Sikkim puts you metres from Chinese soldiers. Indian and Chinese guards stand on either side of the fence at one of the few border pass crossings between the two countries.
Your walk through Bhutan Gate in Jaigaon leads straight into Phuentsholing, Bhutan. The Indian town and the Bhutanese town sit side by side, and the gate is the only thing marking the border.
Your walk across the India-Nepal border at Sunauli needs no visa. The border is open, so Indians and Nepalis cross on foot or by rickshaw in front of a simple gate.
Your fishing boat near Rameswaram passes Katchatheevu, a tiny island that India ceded to Sri Lanka in 1974. It has a church of St Anthony, and the map shows it close to the Indian coast.
Your map of Sir Creek between Gujarat and Pakistan shows a border that runs through a tidal marsh. The water channels shift, and that is why India and Pakistan still disagree on where the line lies.
Your map of the Line of Control stops at a point called NJ9842. Beyond it the agreement says the line runs 'thence north to the glaciers', which leaves the Siachen area undefined.
Your Radcliffe Line in 1947 was drawn in about five weeks by Cyril Radcliffe, a British lawyer who had never been to India before. The line split Punjab and Bengal and the map shows it.

Your visit to Kartarpur lets you see Pakistan's Gurdwara Darbar Sahib from the Indian side. The gurdwara is only a few kilometres from the border, and pilgrims can view it with binoculars or use the special corridor.
Your night at Longwa village in Nagaland puts your bed in two countries. The India-Myanmar border runs through the Angh's (chief's) house, and the villagers hold citizenship of both sides.

Your satellite view of the US-Canada border shows a cleared strip. The International Boundary Commission keeps a six-metre-wide line through forest and mountains, visible from the air as a straight cut.
Your view of the Korean DMZ shows a wildlife haven. The 4 km wide buffer zone between North and South Korea has been nearly empty of people for decades, and cranes and other rare birds live there.
Your boat to Kinmen, Taiwan, takes you to an island only a few kilometres from the Chinese city of Xiamen. You can see the skyline of China from Taiwanese land across the water.
Your walk in Valga-Valka takes you across Estonia and Latvia on foot. One town is split between two countries, and a street, a square and a park all straddle the border.
Your drive on the Thai-Lao Friendship Bridge crosses a river between Thailand and Laos. Thailand drives on the left and Laos on the right, so cars switch sides on the bridge itself.

Your map of Brunei shows a country cut in two pieces by a strip of Malaysia (Limbang), and you cross Malaysia twice, with passport stamps, to drive from one half of Brunei to the other. The countdown runs: 7) Brunei split in two, 6) The Gambia, a thin strip about 25-50 km wide that runs along a river and is surrounded by Senegal on every side except the sea, 5) Azerbaijan's Nakhchivan exclave, cut off from Azerbaijan by Armenia, 4) Angola's Cabinda, cut off from Angola by a strip of DR Congo, 3) Oecusse, East Timor's exclave inside Indonesian West Timor, 2) the Dahagram-Angarpota Bangladeshi enclave inside India, and 1) India's strangest border of all, the Tin Bigha Corridor, a small strip of Indian land leased to Bangladesh so its citizens can reach Dahagram, with a gate that opens and closes at set hours. Each stop is shown as a simple animated map with the odd shape highlighted on screen, and the video ends on a loop back to the hook and a one-line tease for the next video.
